This birth weight, coupled with a gestation period lasting 238 days [tg = 238 days] under the species' typical body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], positions the species firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum among alcelaphin bovids. Newborn calves are precocial and begin standing within minutes of parturition, an adaptive strategy that enhances their ability to follow the maternal herd across the open grassland and woodland savanna habitats that Topi occupy throughout eastern and southern Africa. The relatively long gestation, comparable to that of the closely related hartebeest, allows for substantial foetal organogenesis and neuromuscular development prior to delivery, which is critical for calf survival in an environment where predation pressure from large carnivores such as lions and spotted hyenas is intense. The investment per offspring is thus considerable, setting the stage for the species' slow-paced life history.

As female Topi mature, they reach an adult body mass of 120,000 grams [Wwi = 120,000 grams], while males attain a significantly larger ultimate wet weight of 137,000 grams [Wwi = 137,000 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males outweighing females by approximately fourteen percent, is a common feature among polygynous ungulates where competition for access to breeding territories and receptive females drives selection for increased male body size. The mass differential becomes apparent during the sub-adult stage, as young males continue somatic growth well beyond the age at which females have largely plateaued in their structural development. Such dimorphism has direct implications for the species' social organization, with larger males better able to defend resource-rich lekking territories during the breeding season. Field measurements from multiple populations indicate that these asymptotic masses are achieved after several years of sustained growth, with individuals in highly productive habitats sometimes exceeding these figures under exceptional forage conditions.

This pronounced sex difference in maturation rate—nearly twice as long for males—is consistent with the prolonged period of somatic growth necessary for males to achieve competitive body size before entering the breeding population. Females, by contrast, can begin ovulatory cycles at a younger age, allowing them to reproduce earlier and thus contribute more rapidly to population growth under favorable environmental conditions. The timing of these developmental transitions is mediated by nutritional status, with individuals in high-quality grazing areas reaching puberty several months earlier than those in marginal habitats.

The post-weaning period is characterized by high mortality rates, as young animals must navigate the dual challenges of acquiring adequate nutrition while remaining vigilant against predators without the constant protective proximity of their mothers. This conservative reproductive output is offset by high adult survival rates and the extended reproductive lifespan afforded by the species' maximum longevity, enabling females to produce multiple offspring over their lifetime despite the constraints imposed by a lengthy gestation and extended period of maternal care. Comparative analyses with other alcelaphin antelopes suggest that this annual reproductive rhythm is shaped by the pronounced seasonality of rainfall and forage quality in the savanna ecosystems that Topi inhabit throughout their geographic range.
